summary: Describes NPTv6, a stateless way to swap one IPv6 network prefix for another as packets cross a boundary. Each inside address maps one-to-one to an outside address, giving some of the address independence of IPv4 NAT while keeping end-to-end reachability at the network layer. It is an Experimental protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: Network Prefix Translation for IPv6 (NPTv6) changes a packet's local IPv6 prefix as the packet crosses a translator. It works in both directions without keeping per-connection state, while preserving the address relationship needed for end-to-end communication.

questions: how does ipv6 prefix translation work
subtitle: A stateless IPv6 method for mapping one network prefix to another.

tldr.problem: A network may want to change its external IPv6 prefix without renumbering the addresses it uses internally.
tldr.mechanism: NPTv6 replaces the local prefix in each packet address and uses a checksum-neutral adjustment, without tracking individual connections.
tldr.outcome: The RFC defines NPTv6 as an Experimental function and warns that it does not provide the security benefit associated with traditional NAT.

today: RFC 6296 is Experimental. It defines a stateless IPv6 prefix-translation function and notes that the function does not itself provide firewall protection.

sections.title: Address Independence for IPv6 Networks
sections.content:
A network may want to change its upstream provider or external prefix without changing the addresses configured on its internal systems. NPTv6 is designed to provide this address independence by mapping an internal prefix to an external prefix.

The RFC describes NPTv6 as transport-agnostic for protocols whose checksums do not cover the IP header or use the TCP/UDP/DCCP pseudo-header. It notes that translation still has architectural and security trade-offs.
sections.plainLanguage: NPTv6 lets an organization change the prefix it presents outside its network while keeping its internal prefix. It changes the address prefix, not the transport ports.

sections.title: Translating in Both Directions
sections.content:
For an outbound packet, the translator replaces the source address's internal prefix with the external prefix. For an inbound packet, it replaces the destination address's external prefix with the matching internal prefix.

The remaining address information identifies the corresponding node. The mapping is algorithmic and two-way, so the translator does not need per-node or per-flow state to map addresses in either direction.
sections.plainLanguage: Going out, the translator changes the source prefix. Coming in, it changes the destination prefix back to the internal one, using the same address mapping.

sections.title: Checksum-Neutral Mapping
sections.content:
Changing an IPv6 address can affect a transport checksum that includes the IPv6 pseudo-header. NPTv6 adjusts another part of the address to offset the prefix change, so the checksum calculation remains the same.

This checksum-neutral property means that a translator does not have to rewrite the TCP or UDP header to repair its checksum. NPTv6 also does not change port numbers or other transport parameters.
sections.plainLanguage: The address change is balanced by a second address adjustment. This keeps the relevant checksum unchanged, so the translator can leave the transport header alone.

sections.title: Applications and Security Limits
sections.content:
The RFC discusses application effects, prefix planning, and the behavior expected from a translator. Applications that place IP addresses inside their own data may need special consideration when those addresses are translated.

NPTv6 does not provide the security benefit that some deployments associate with IPv4 NAT. The RFC says a firewall is needed if that benefit is desired, and notes that some protocols that authenticate IP addresses cannot have those addresses translated.
sections.plainLanguage: NPTv6 changes addresses but does not act as a firewall. Applications or security methods that rely on the original address may need separate handling.
